articles.title: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
articles.snippet: Tons of chilled and frozen food was spoiled last month as fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets heated up.
articles.full_text:
France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
- Published
France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers across the country last month.
Foreign Minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barrot said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding those who were responsible would be hit with sanctions.
Iran has yet to respond officially, but some Iranian media outlets have dismissed the allegations as baseless.
The French hacking, which led to the destruction of tons of frozen and chilled food in France was followed by a similar attack against supermarkets across several other European countries. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".
He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".
France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.
The Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with the IRGC as well as his two deputies.
Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.
In recent weeks, a number of commentators and politicians in Iran have argued that the country should extend any retaliation beyond the Middle East if the US and Israel resume the war they started earlier this year.
If the IRGC carried out the cyber-attacks, it remains unclear whether they were part of Iran's deterrence strategy.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.
More than 100 of CoopÃ©rative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from IntermarchÃ© and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.
Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.
Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.
In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.
The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber-attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.
Additional reporting by Farshad Bayan, BBC Persian.

articles.title: France blames Iran for fridge cyberattacks, says some caused fires
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: In the first attribution since the October attacks, the French authorities identified the perpetrators as part of Shahid Kaveh, an IRGC cyber unit previously linked to attacks on industrial controllers at U.S. water utilities.
articles.full_text:
France blames Iran for fridge cyberattacks, says some caused fires
French authorities on Monday accused Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of a cyberattack sabotaging refrigeration systems at around 700 French grocery stores last month, causing what it said were extensive food losses and at least 15 fires.
The accusation was made in a five-page report published Monday by France’s Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre, which brings together the national cybersecurity agency ANSSI, the military’s cyber command and the DGSE and DGSI intelligence services.
In the first attribution since the October attacks, the French authorities identified the perpetrators as part of Shahid Kaveh, an IRGC cyber unit previously linked to attacks on industrial controllers at U.S. water utilities.
France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot told reporters at a G7 ministerial meeting in Paris that he could confirm the IRGC was responsible for the fridge attacks, describing the sabotage as unprecedented in its scale and aggressiveness.
France has summoned Iran’s ambassador and Barrot said the country will pursue European sanctions against those responsible.
Victims of the first wave of attacks included stores operated by large chains, as well as smaller businesses including butchers, a slaughterhouse and cooperative food-processing plants.
ANSSI said it also identified the Iranian hackers simultaneously targeting Schneider Electric equipment at several small hydroelectric facilities, although the disruption to those systems was described as moderate.
The cybersecurity agency’s report does not address the second such wave of attacks against refrigeration systems in early November. That wave hit businesses in at least 11 European countries, including British meat suppliers and three sites operated by France's national blood service.
The Paris Prosecutor’s Office said at the same time Monday it was opening a judicial investigation against the head of the Shahid Kaveh unit, as well as two of its deputies and other suspects yet to be identified. It has requested international arrest warrants for the suspects, according to prosecutor Laure Beccuau.
Outing the cyber saboteurs
French investigators identified a range of evidence linking the attacks to Shahid Kaveh including Farsi text artefacts, tooling and infrastructure used in reconnaissance on other industrial equipment.
An annex to the report names and pictures Hamid Reza Lashgarian, head of the IRGC Electronic and Cyber Center, and Mahdi Lashgarian and Reza Salarvand as commanders of Shahid Kaveh.
Earlier this year, the U.S. Defense Department, FBI, National Security Agency and other federal agencies identified Shahid Kaveh as another name for the CyberAv3ngers group, which it linked to attacks targeting operational technology (OT) devices and causing disruptions across multiple U.S. critical infrastructure sectors.
The U.S. State Department had previously offered rewards of up to $10 million for information on six IRGC officials connected to the group’s 2023 attacks on U.S. water utilities. It names both of the Lashgarians. Salarvand had not previously been publicly identified.
In September, the State Department announced a further reward for information on Amir Yaryab, whom it accused of overseeing CyberAv3ngers operations.
The ANSSI report separately attributed several earlier attacks against French interests to another IRGC unit, Shahid Shoostari, also known as Emennet Pasargad, including the defacement of the website of satirical newspaper Charlie Hebdo.
The unit also attempted to hijack digital advertising displays during the 2024 Paris Olympics, compromising a French company managing video display terminals and attempting to use them to show images condemning Israeli athletes’ participation in the Games.
The intrusion was discovered before the images could be displayed. Investigators traced related material to a Persian-language Instagram account, two X accounts and an Iranian news website. They also identified connections from two Iranian internet service provider IP addresses.
French authorities linked Shahid Shoostari to an earlier plan to target Charlie Hebdo in 2020, following the newspaper's republication of cartoons depicting the Prophet Muhammad.
ANSSI said both Shahid Shoostari and Shahid Kaveh operate under the IRGC’s Electronic and Cyber Center. The agency described the incidents as part of a campaign of destabilization against French interests dating back at least six years.
Iran routinely denies conducting malicious cyber operations. It had not publicly responded to France’s allegations by Monday evening.
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.snippet: The share price dropped wiped hundreds of billions of dollars from the value of Nvidia.
articles.full_text:
Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
- Published
Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 4% by close of trade on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.
Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.
However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying "allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".
Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report, external.
The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.
Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.
The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.
Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee last week asked Jensen Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information," congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter.
"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."
After Nvidia's investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Jensen Huang to continue leading the firm.
US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".
However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (Â£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.
While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened on a positive note on Monday after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting.
But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so central to the AI industry.
"Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.
Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993.
Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but he decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.
Huang's position vulnerable unlike other tech bosses
A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Jensen Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.
Jensen Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him.
He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision.
By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.
Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."
The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.
Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.
What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy
- Published5 hours ago
Nvidia chips have been a major focus of the AI race between the US and China and the White House has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.
But Jensen Huang has been against restricting the sale of Nvidia's chips to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.
Additional reporter by Samira Hussain, North America business correspondent.

articles.title: Trump questions midterm elections integrity after previously accepting results
articles.snippet: Trump made the claims, without evidence, on Truth Social on Monday.
articles.full_text:
Trump questions midterm elections integrity after previously accepting results
- Published
US President Donald Trump has questioned the legitimacy of the midterm election results in which Republicans suffered sweeping losses, days after saying he would accept the outcome.
"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong?" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.
This appeared to contradict what he told the New York Times on election night that he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results.
Democrats retook both chambers of Congress in last week's elections. State and local officials across the US said voting had been mostly problem-free.
Some key races, including Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi, have yet to be called.
In the Truth Social post, Trump made vague claims about polling, voting "dumps", and "machines" without providing specific evidence of what this referred to and whether he believed there had been error or wrongdoing.
The reporting of vote counts on election night proceeded as normal, according to Charles Stewart III, a political scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).
"We saw across the nation the standard patterns we see in terms of when the votes are reported," he said.
Stewart added that in some states, like Florida and Georgia, some initial reporting of results happens quickly because they already have the results of early and mail ballots.
Trump has previously attempted to cast doubts on the integrity of elections he has lost, although he himself was not on the ballot in the midterms.
"We would have won easily if I was on the ballot," Trump told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, after it was confirmed his party had lost both the Senate and the House.
Surveys ahead of the election from several pollsters and news outlets suggested that Republicans could lose seats in both the House and Senate.
As it stands, Democrats have won 54 US Senate seats and 254 US House seats in the midterms, giving them comfortable majorities in both chambers of Congress even as counting continues in some races, like in Alaska and Mississippi.
"State laws and practicalities are such that some states will just take longer to count," said Ruth Greenwood, director of the Election Law Clinic at Harvard Law School.
"That doesn't mean anything nefarious is occurringâwe just need to trust local election officials to count every vote and tell us the results when they are done."
The outcome has been clear since election night. Trump told the New York Times then: "We'll, you know, look forward to working with [Democrats]", adding: "We'll probably work something out."
He has also offered his own analysis of why Republicans lost, acknowledging on Fox News that the Iran war had contributed to the defeat.
"People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that," he said.
Vice-President JD Vance has also blamed the Iran war, which began in February and which has severely disrupted global oil and gas supplies - causing costs to soar, as the reason their party lost the election.
In the run-up to the midterms, Trump made claims about widespread voting fraud, despite evidence that it is rare.
He and his allies alleged for months that the 2020 presidential election, which he lost to former President Joe Biden, had been rigged against him. His lawyers and allies spent weeks attempting to litigate the results, but courts repeatedly struck them down.
The justice department during his administration has made unprecedented attempts to exert more federal control over elections - a power the Constitution primarily delegates to individual states.
Days before these midterms, it filed controversial lawsuits in federal courts challenging the count and certification of votes in states like California and Alaska, but judges ruled against them in nearly all instances.
Election law experts, state officials, and local elections offices told the BBC they had spent months preparing for a scenario in which the White House or election sceptics questioned the votes' legitimacy.
Despite the intense focus around election integrity on both sides of the debate, top state and local election officials have reported a mostly smooth process so far for the 2026 midterms.
Extreme weather did force some location closures, and a handful of reported administrative or technical issues slowed the process in some local jurisdictions.

Turkey steel factory blast kills at least 17 people
- Published
At least 17 people have died and 12 others have been injured in an explosion at an iron and steel factory near the port city of Izmir in western Turkey.
All those killed and injured were workers at the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga, one of the country's leading steel producers, authorities said. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the facility and a towering column of smoke rising into the air.
The local governor said the blast happened around midday after a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a furnace below.
Workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey, the Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society organisation, said.
President Recep Tayyip ErdoÄan originally said the death toll was 16, but later Health Minister Kemal MemiÅoÄlu announced that one of those who had been critically injured had later died of their injuries, taking the toll to 17.
Eyewitnesses at the scene of the incident said the explosion shook the ground, with one person initially believing an earthquake had struck.
In a statement, the company that runs the factory said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance work on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces.
Izmir Governor SÃ¼leyman Elban told media that some people were believed to still be under the rubble.
Speaking after a cabinet meeting on Monday, ErdoÄan confirmed the deaths and said investigations were under way, while search and rescue operations continued.
At least five people have been arrested, according BBC News's Turkish service, citing local media reports.
The Habas plant is in the Izmir district of Aliaga which is a major port and one of Turkey's main shipbreaking hubs.

articles.title: Republican congressman to force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth
articles.snippet: The effort will likely fail, but Representative Thomas Massie wants to push Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.
articles.full_text:
Republican congressman to force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth
- Published
A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has violated the US Constitution.
"By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Representative Thomas Massie said.
The effort will likely fail, given Republicans will remain in power in Congress until January. But Massie says he wants to push President Donald Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.
Hegseth, who will hold a news conference on Tuesday about Massie's move, said he was not concerned.
Massie formally introduced the articles of impeachment in a resolution on the House floor on Monday afternoon.
"I'm doing this because it's the right thing to do," the outgoing congressman told reporters after introducing the articles.
When asked by reporters about the impending resolution earlier on Monday, Hegseth said: "We're not worried about that.
He adding he would hold a news conference Tuesday morning "on that very topic". Hegseth's last news conference was in May.
Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it started nearly nine months ago. He is known across the country for also pushing the administration to release federal files on the deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The Kentucky congressman first introduced impeachment articles in September and is now pressing for a vote in the wake of Republicans losing control of both the House and Senate in last week's midterm elections. He has said his push to rid the administration of Hegseth is meant to prevent a Democrat spectacle next year.
"My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie also said in a statement. "They will hold hearings and trials."
"President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate," he also said.
Impeaching a cabinet secretary is very rare. The impeachment must be approved by both chambers for the secretary to be removed from office. As with presidential impeachments, the House would first hold a vote on charges against Hegseth and the Senate then would conduct a trial to decide whether to acquit or convict.
The House has voted to impeach only two cabinet members in US history, but the Senate did not convict either one.
Now Massie has introduced his resolution, Speaker of the House Mike Johnson must schedule a time to consider it within two days. Along with voting on the resolution directly, the House has the options to vote to refer it to committee or to set it aside.
Massie will likely have the support of House Democrats, with that party's leader, Hakeem Jeffries, saying on Sunday that he is a "hard yes" on impeachment. But Massie would still need to win over members of his own party.
Massie told reporters he was not sure if the measure had sufficient backing to pass.
Peter Loge, a professor of public affairs at George Washington University, told the BBC that the impeachment measure is "likely to pass the House because the Republican majority is so slim".
"And there are enough angry Republicans that more than enough Republicans are gonna simply not show up to vote," he added.
Currently, there are 218 Republicans and 214 Democrats in the House.
The Senate requires a two-thirds vote to convict, a threshold that would be hard to meet in the current congressional term. When the Democrats take over in January, they still will not have enough seats to convict Hegseth without Republican support.
In the articles, Massie also accused Hegseth of intimidating critics of the Trump administration, kidnapping foreign leaders and ignoring congressional War Powers resolutions.
The House has passed a War Powers resolution - a measure seeking to halt Trump from taking further military action in Iran - multiple times this year, with Massie's support. The Senate also passed a War Powers resolution over the summer.
Loge said the chances that Hegseth would survive until the end of Trump's term are "pretty slim", but he expected Hegseth to be ousted instead of impeached.
"Secretary Hegseth is a big personality, and I'm not sure I'd want to be a big personality that's drawing attention from President Trump these days," Loge said. "That's not a way to guarantee job security."

articles.title: Nine Zimbabweans caught allegedly trying to leave South Africa to fight in Ukraine
articles.snippet: Hundreds of people from different African countries have been recruited to fight for Russia, according to Ukraine.
articles.full_text:
Nine Zimbabweans caught allegedly trying to leave South Africa to fight in Ukraine
- Published
Nine Zimbabweans have been arrested in South Africa after they were caught allegedly trying to leave the country to fight in the war between Russia and the Ukraine, police say.
The group, aged between 20 and 26, were arrested in and around Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team on Sunday evening.
They were caught as they were "preparing to board flights out of the country", authorities added, but their final destination is unclear.
They have been charged with contravening South Africa's Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act, which outlaws mercenary activity without government permission.
Police said five people were arrested at South Africa's biggest airport, OR Tambo, and another four at a hotel in Bruma, east of Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team that involved Interpol.
All nine later appeared in court, according to state prosecutors.
The police statement added that the involvement of Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies indicated that the suspects had also allegedly violated laws in their respective home countries, prompting cooperation with South African authorities.
They have also not said whether the group allegedly intended to fight for Russia or Ukraine nor provided details of the organisations allegedly involved in facilitating their travel.
Citizens of several African countries, including Kenya, Ghana and South Africa, have gone to fight for Russia in Ukraine - some they had been duped and had not realised where they were going.
A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated earlier this year that more than 1,700 people from 36 countries in Africa have been recruited to fight for Russia.
Kenya at the time estimated that 252 citizens had been illegally conscripted in Russia. In March, Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi visited Moscow to address the issue.
He said at the time that an agreement had been reached to stop recruiting Kenyan nationals.
In March, Zimbabwe said that 15 of its nationals had been killed after being recruited to fight for Russia in Ukraine, with more than 60 still trapped on the frontlines.
The previous month, South Africa secured the return of 17 South Africans who were allegedly tricked into joining the war.
In December last year, South African authorities arrested five people, including a journalist, for allegedly recruiting people to join the war.
Ukraine has also been recruiting foreign nationals, including from Africa.

Russia's leading independent newspaper closes after eviction
Russia's leading independent newspaper has closed after being evicted from its offices and facing pressure from authorities.
For 30 years, Novaya Gazeta published investigations into corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power in the country.
On Monday, the team behind the newspaper had a final editorial meeting before packing up their belongings and leaving.
The Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia's media was highly diverse and that the newspaper's closure was part of "a standard rotational process".
The BBC spoke to its co-founder Dmitry Muratov, a Nobel Peace Prize winner, about the closure.

articles.title: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case - media reports
articles.snippet: The ruling means prosecutors can pursue the case, meaning they could reduce charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.
articles.full_text:
Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case - media reports
- Published
A Massachusetts judge has denied motions to dismiss the murder case of Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of murdering her three children, according to local US media.
The judge's ruling comes after Clancy's defence team requested dismissal of the case after her first trial ended in a mistrial in September, when a 12-person jury failed to reach a consensus.
The ruling clears the way for prosecutors to pursue the case. They could reduce the charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.
Clancy has not denied killing her children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional.
Clancy's defence team had filed three motions, including one to dismiss the case against her due to double jeopardy - a legal standard that says a person cannot be tried for the same crime twice.
Her lawyers argued that Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the August murder trial, acted prematurely when he declared a mistrial on 4 September, saying that he should have sought a viable alternative.
In his ruling on Monday, Sullivan said that a retrial would not unconstitutionally subject her to double jeopardy, according to Reuters news agency.
Sullivan also denied a motion to see records of the lone holdout juror in the case and to question the juror under oath.
The judge scheduled a hearing for 16 November to discuss when to hold a second trial. He has previously suggested it could begin in March.

The island has been split since 1974, when Turkiye invaded and seized the northern part after a coup by the Greeks.
Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot leaders have agreed to open two new border crossings, coordinate emergency responses, and share archival materials as part of a United Nations-backed effort to resume peace talks on the divided island.
Greek Cypriot leader Nikos Christodoulides and Turkish Cypriot leader Tufan Erhurman jointly met with United Nations special envoy Maria Angela Holguin on Monday in the UN-controlled buffer zone that splits the island. The agreement is the first concrete sign of detente between the rivals after nearly a decade of deadlock.

Africans and others continue to be recruited to fight for Russia in its war on Ukraine.
South African police have arrested nine foreign nationals suspected of seeking to travel from the country to fight in Russia’s war on Ukraine.
The suspects were arrested late Sunday night at OR Tambo Airport in Johannesburg and at a nearby hotel, police said. Numerous reports have detailed how people from Africa and other continents have been tricked into travelling to Russia only to be forced to join Moscow’s grinding war on its neighbour.

articles.title: Dutch firm Optics11 in talks with navies on secretive underwater listening tech
articles.snippet: For underwater use, the company’s fiber-optic sensing can detect an oil tanker at 100 kilometers, the CEO said.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — Dutch startup Optics11 is in talks with dozens of navies about using its optical-fiber sensing technology for underwater monitoring and threat detection, with between five and ten navies already signed on as clients, Chief Executive Officer Paul Heiden said.
The company will have around 35 paid trials this year with navies testing its tech, Heiden told Defense News at the Euronaval maritime-defense exhibition outside Paris on Nov. 4. Those tests include several for the German Navy through various local defense-prime partners, as well as for Sweden, the United Kingdom, Belgium and France.
Optics11 beams light through optic fiber to detect acoustic vibrations underwater, either for static monitoring or towed array sensors, and Heiden said the technology is more sensitive and has higher resolution than passive sonar using piezoelectric detection. The firm is developing a towed array for the Royal Netherlands Navy for the future Orka-class submarines ordered from France’s Naval Group.
“Every navy knows that this is the technology of the future,” Heiden said.
The Optics11 portfolio includes OptiBarrier, a stationary seabed monitoring system, and OptiArray, a towed array that can be deployed from submarines and unmanned vessels.
The CEO said Optics11 will probably raise funds next year, and do so at a unicorn valuation, referring to a startup valuation that exceeds US$1 billion. The startup raised around €100 million in funding in the past 15 months, through equity financing as well as €25 million in venture debt financing from the European Investment Bank, according to Heiden.
Optics11 is not yet profitable, and Heiden expects the company to become cash-flow positive in 2028.
The CEO said nearly everything around underwater data collection is “extremely secret” and a lot of information around navies using Optics11 technology is classified. He said the company’s products are currently deployed in war zones, “and yeah, I can’t say anything about that either.”
Optics11 has a technology lead in optical-fiber sensing after years of deep-tech research that would make it hard for a competitor to enter the market with anything similar, at least in markets including Europe, the Middle East and South East Asia, according to the CEO. He said he’s not sure where China or the United States stand in terms of developing similar technology.
The optical fiber technology used by Optics11 was initially used in medical applications, and is so sensitive it can detect cells dividing, according to Heiden. For underwater use, the company’s fiber-optic sensing can detect an oil tanker at 100 kilometers, the CEO said.
Most of the company’s “really crucial developments” of the past seven to eight years rely on trade secrets rather than patents to protect intellectual property, due to the sensitivity of the technology, Heiden said. The Dutch government provides specialists to help the firm protect its data, and vets company employees working on classified technology.
“You can’t publish this, you can’t patent it, so it all has to be kept secret, and we’re getting great help from the Dutch government to keep it truly secret,” Heiden said.
Heiden said he holds monthly discussions within the company to make sure employees disclose if, for example, they are being threatened or their families are being put under pressure.
The Optics11 strategy is to build and sell its products locally, both to reduce supply chain risk for customers and because governments want to see their defense investments flow back into their own economies. “We’ll identify who the local prime is, and then we’ll work with them to fully integrate our technology,” Heiden said.
Should Optics11 raise money next year, the funds would partly be used to finance its expansion in the Middle East and South East Asia, where the firm is opening offices and hiring staff with “the goal to operate in a highly localized manner.”
Optics11 already works with partners including Saab, Rheinmetall, Fincantieri, Thales and Exail, Heiden said. The firm is a technology supplier for Ocean Infinity, which was picked by the U.K. to manage the anti-submarine surveillance program as part of Britain’s Atlantic Bastion initiative.
The higher sensitivity of optical fiber compared to traditional sonar translates into a “much larger” amount of sensing data per cubic nautical mile, which Optics11 processes using its own edge-computing software, the CEO said.
“Initially I thought we could work with a partner, but our data density is so high that we couldn’t derive any value from third-party sonar processing software,” Heiden said. “That’s why we started building that kind of software ourselves, and it’s now an integral part of our offering. So we’ve really built a serious R&D operation here.”
Artificial intelligence has helped cut down the effort required to develop software, with Optics11 now employing ten developers, according to Heiden, who said that as recently as 2024 and 2025 he had still been planning for around 60 to 80 people in software development.
“That means you can invest that money in acoustic specialists who have a much better understanding of how sound travels through the ocean, which will allow you to optimize your algorithms much faster and make them more precise for sandy seabeds, rocky seabeds, that sort of thing,” the CEO said.
Optics11 has been working with the Royal Netherlands Navy for at least eight years, with the Dutch military providing millions of euros in subsidies, steering the direction of development, as well as testing the company’s technology on submarines, according to Heiden.
Attracting funding was still complicated for Optics11 in early 2024 due to financial firms excluding defense firms from investment portfolios, something which “completely changed” in November that same year after a vessel dragged its anchor in the Baltic Sea, severing several cables, Heiden said.
“All of a sudden all kinds of investment firms were willing to work with us,” Heiden said. “That was really driven by our ability to listen underwater, companies were prepared to seriously invest in that. So seriously, in fact, that over the last fifteen months we’ve raised about 100 million, which is quite a substantial amount.”

articles.title: Firm bets on converted fishing trawlers to tackle Russian submarines in the Arctic
articles.snippet: The company’s Arctic Hunter idea involves an industry-standard 56-meter trawler design whose fish-processing innards are ripped out and replaced with autonomy features.
articles.full_text:
COLOGNE, Germany — Norway’s Kongsberg Maritime is pitching an unmanned fishing vessel design converted with technology to spot Russian submarines in the Arctic region on behalf of the British Royal Navy.
The company’s Arctic Hunter concept involves an industry-standard 56-meter trawler design with its fish-processing innards ripped out and replaced with autonomy features, allowing the craft to comb the ocean unattended for roughly 60 days at a time, a company spokesman told Defense News.
The ships would carry submarine-hunting sonar technology made by Thales UK, as well as secure communications capabilities, Kongsberg Maritime said in a Nov. 9 announcement. Some aspects of the ship, like the propeller, are slated for redesign to reduce its acoustic signature to avoid interfering with the onboard sonar, according to the company.
The proposal responds to a U.K. requirement for unmanned vessels that can assist anti-submarine warfare. The envisioned British Type 92 ships, as they are known in Royal Navy nomenclature, harken back to a World War 2-era idea that saw large numbers of relatively inexpensive converted whaler-type vessels protect U.K. warships against Nazi Germany’s submarine fleet.
Kongsberg Maritime’s concept of operations for the Arctic Hunter involves a flotilla of 10 ships based and supported somewhere “west of the Bear Gap,” a stretch of the Arctic Ocean between Svalbard and Norway through which Russian submarines must cross on the way to the open Atlantic, a company spokesman said.
Locating the drones’ hub near their area of operations beats having to travel the distance all the way from Britain, the logic goes.
The future Type 92 vessels are central to the British idea of a hybrid Navy with crewed and uncrewed ships working in concert on specific tasks. In anti-submarine warfare, surface drones like Arctic Hunter would assist future Type 26 frigates, being built by BAE Systems for the U.K., Australia, Canada and Norway, in their missions.
Kongsberg Maritime, recently incorporated as its own entity from the parent Kongsberg defense firm, says it understands the task of developing ships for Britain’s hybrid Navy as a “maritime engineering” problem rather than a naval armament problem, a company spokesman said. That’s because the commercial world already has plenty of hardy, proven ship types suited to harsh North Atlantic conditions that simply need to be retooled for unmanned operations.
If picked to build Type 92 ships, Kongsberg Maritime says it would do so in the United Kingdom.

articles.title: Neros to expand domestic drone production with $450M Pentagon loan
articles.snippet: The company is a frontrunner in a Defense Department competition to find the best quality, most affordable small drone for combat.
articles.full_text:
California-based drone maker Neros Technologies, a frontrunner in a Defense Department competition for small drones for combat, received a $450 million conditional loan from the DoD to expand domestic manufacturing of small drone components.
In an interview with Military Times, Ross Pederson, Neros’ head of growth, called the expansion of the U.S. small drone industry “a huge benefit to the American taxpayer.”
“I don’t think you have to squint too hard to convince yourself that small drones are going to be very, very important in the future of warfare,” he said. “And if you look at the status quo ante, which is that 99% of them are made in China, that’s not a tenable place for the U.S. to be.”
The Defense Department’s Office of Strategic Capital, or OSC, provided the loan. Neros said it will commit an additional $165 million to the expansion, which brings the total investment to $615 million.
Pederson argued that OSC loans to Neros and drone maker PDW, which received an $820 million loan in July, will strengthen the U.S. industry. China has “completely dominated” the sector, he said, with Chinese companies supplying the vast majority of components used to assemble drones.
Explaining its reasoning for giving Neros the loan, David Lorch, director of the OSC and senior advisor to the deputy secretary of defense, said the company “has already demonstrated an ability to design, manufacture and deliver exceptional small unmanned aircraft systems.”
The company is one of the leaders in the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance Program, a competition that seeks to find the best quality, most affordable small drone for combat.
“OSC’s investment will turbocharge Neros’ ability to manufacture drones and components critical for the production of drone systems,” Lorch added in a statement.
The federal government has taken other steps over the past year to expand the domestic small-drone industry, ranging from launching high-profile competitions to imposing tariffs on imported drone components.
Although the Trump administration’s broad use of tariffs on consumer goods has drawn criticism, drone industry experts say the import duties have helped encourage companies to seek domestic alternatives.
In October, Brett Velicovich — author of Drone Warrior, which documents his military experience using small drones in combat, and head of drone company POWERUS — told Military Times that tariffs on drone components were “one of the smartest things the White House has done in decades.”
He argued that the U.S. had put “handcuffs” on its domestic industry through export restrictions, while China faced fewer constraints. That imbalance, he said, helped China capture the overwhelming majority of the global market for small drones and their components.
The tariffs have created a bottleneck for components that has “been hard on everyone,” Velicovich said. But he argued that they have also pushed domestic companies to “now focus on (National Defense Authorization Act)-compliant parts” and “forces all of us to find new supply chains.”
“In the end, it’s what’s good for America because we can’t continue to be reliant on China. We can’t continue to be reliant on those systems,” he said.
But tariffs aren’t necessarily the main driver of domestic sourcing for military customers, according to Pederson. The Defense Department has long been prohibited from purchasing drones containing electronic components from certain foreign countries, including China, he said.
“When it comes to that specific customer set, the tariffs aren’t necessarily the driving factor. It’s really the prohibition that the Department of War has on purchasing Chinese electronics,” he said.
Before receiving the loan, Pederson explained, Neros didn’t manufacture its own components. Instead, it contracted other companies to manufacture parts that it then used to assemble drones. That is expected to change as the company expands its domestic production capabilities.
Neros has already expanded its in-house motor production and will soon begin manufacturing surface-mount technology components, which are used to populate circuit boards, Pederson said.
“By late next year, somewhere in the like 80% by dollar value of the drone should be made in-house, like in the same physical space where the drones are being assembled,” he said.
Pederson declined to provide specifics about the loan’s terms, including its interest rate and repayment timeline, but he said it is not subject to loan forgiveness and that the Defense Department has manufacturing goals for the company.
“They’re all centered on making these components in the United States and making them available broadly to the market, not just to ourselves,” he said.
