articles.title: Swiss neutrality proponents challenge arms firms in vote on easing of exports
articles.snippet: Swiss voters will decide on Nov. 29 whether to block a bill relaxing curbs on weapons exports, in a referendum that touches on Switzerland's evolving neutral tradition.
articles.full_text:
ZURICH — Swiss voters will decide on Nov. 29 whether to block a bill relaxing curbs on weapons exports, in a referendum that raises questions about Switzerland’s evolving neutral tradition and is strongly opposed by the arms industry.
Switzerland follows the 1907 Hague Conventions on neutrality, which prevent it participating in armed conflicts unless directly threatened, or providing military support to any of the parties.
Yet a stance that largely held throughout the Cold War has begun to change since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 prompted Switzerland to deepen its defense ties with European partners and the transatlantic NATO alliance.
Polls suggest the referendum, proposed by a coalition of left-wing parties including Social Democrats, the Greens and others, could go either way.
Some right-wingers have also split from the Swiss People’s Party (SVP) to oppose the amendment, which cannot come into force until the referendum is held.
“In future, Swiss war material could in certain cases be passed to belligerent states,” said Fabian Molina, a lawmaker for the leftist Social Democrats. “That would violate neutrality.”
The amendment is intended to allow arms shipments to 36 Western countries, even if they are involved in active armed conflicts, albeit not for use in those conflicts. Ukraine is not included, however.
It also scraps a requirement for countries to sign a non-re-export declaration upon purchase.
Bern had blocked several countries from sending previously purchased Swiss-made ammunition and combat vehicles to Ukraine, and Germany subsequently excluded Swiss firms from procurement deals, while Denmark and the Netherlands halted orders.
The amendment would, however, not apply to weaponry bought on the previous terms, or bought with the intention of immediately sending it to a third party – thus still excluding Ukraine.
Center Party lawmaker Reto Nause said the law needed to be overhauled to reflect a more dangerous international environment.
“We’re facing a level of threat we haven’t seen since the Second World War,” he said. “Part of being able to defend yourself is having a domestic arms industry, having some production capacity and above all know-how in key technologies.”
The non-re-export declaration would deter NATO countries from buying Swiss armaments because they wanted to be able to share weapons if the alliance was attacked, Nause said.
The affected manufacturers include Germany’s Rheinmetall, which builds anti-drone defense systems in Switzerland, French defense group Thales, small-arms maker SIG Sauer, and more than 100 other companies.
Weapons made in Switzerland
Switzerland was the world’s 17th-largest arms exporter over the past 10 years, according to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
The sector employs 14,000 people and last year, its exports were worth around $1.15 billion.
Manufacturers fear for the future if the law is not amended, arguing that the domestic market is too small, and their supporters say there are another 154,000 jobs in companies making “dual use” products – for military or civilian purposes.
“This is decisive, it’s really ‘go’ or ‘no go’ for the future of the Swiss arms industry,” said Matthias Zoller, general secretary of the Swiss Aeronautics, Security and Defence Association, which represents the industry.
He said it was crucial for Switzerland to have its own armaments industry but, if exports were excessively restricted, manufacturers could simply move abroad.
And if Switzerland could no longer sell arms abroad, it could expect to go to the back of the line for buying new systems or even components from other countries, he said.
Green Party lawmaker Gerhard Andrey said ceding control of where Swiss arms go was “not a neutral choice,” and noted that exports were just below record level last year, despite the restrictions.
Mirjam Hostetmann, leader of the youth wing of the Social Democrats, said relaxing the law could lead to Swiss weapons increasingly being used in civil wars or by rogue governments.
“It’s an illusion to believe that more weapons will guarantee more peace,” she said. “Nobody benefits from these changes apart from the arms industry.”

articles.title: The next breakthrough is software built on the battlefield by agentic bots
articles.snippet: [Sponsored] Autonomous agents and mission-specific software promise faster responses to emerging threats.
articles.full_text:
Super Intelligence (SI) is not a new tool for the US military. However, it is rapidly evolving and offering new capabilities and challenges, moving from large language models that are limited by the data sets they were trained on to agentic SI models that can act with autonomy.
Building the SI tools needed to keep pace with rapidly changing battlefield threats will require understanding that time is of the essence, as countermeasures and defenses cannot take months or years to build. With SI tools becoming available outside of classified settings, nation-states and rogue actors can adopt new technology to quickly develop new vectors of attack, said Garrett Berntsen, chief AI officer, Accenture Federal Services.
“Today, powerful frontier models are often open-sourced within months,” he said. “That means adversarial actors or a teenager in a basement will soon have tools capable of synthesizing vulnerabilities into potent cyberweapons. Our adversaries aren’t just processing data faster, they are acting faster. Defensively, we are on a ticking clock to harden our systems using these same capabilities.”
That ticking clock makes it hard for humans to keep pace with constantly changing threats. Autonomy will be needed, so agentic capabilities can do more than large language models can while still giving a human ultimate decision-making authority allows the US and its allies to maintain a speed advantage.
Human in the lead
Every unit of the military operates according to rules of engagement (ROE), which vary based on the situation. The ROE that a warfighter is operating under in Operation Epic Fury is different from the ROE for forces in Afghanistan. There is no one-size-fits-all standard, and that is true for using SI-powered tools, as well.
Pre-determined guardrails prevent SI systems from operating with free reign while enabling different levels of autonomy based on their task. Agents sorting through reams of data to identify patterns or changes in surveillance imagery may be given close to full autonomy, while drones tasked with following a convoy or tracking an individual target may be operating under stricter parameters.
The key is properly structuring control mechanisms to enable SI systems to operate efficiently while maintaining human authority without bottlenecks. If a human is needed to approve every function, then SI systems do not offer a speed advantage. Adjusting parameters to meet a specific task (e.g., identify what has changed in satellite imagery over the last 72 hours) or a function of a task (e.g., follow this vehicle even if it veers off from the convoy, but do not engage without human authority) is necessary to ensure operations are carried out without unnecessary delays while keeping humans in the ultimate decision-making roles.
In lower-risk scenarios such as supply chain logistics or route planning, SI systems can be granted a high level of autonomy with humans auditing the outcomes to see how to adjust in the future. In scenarios involving strikes or critical target identification, humans maintain more control to ensure an SI-powered system doesn’t act without authority, said Berntsen.
“The goal of agentic isn’t to replace human judgment; it’s to clear away the cognitive noise so that when the human makes a decision, it is based on synthesized, real-time ground truth rather than overwhelming data overload.”
Modernizing effectively
Building new tools or adapting existing tools to meet new challenges requires modernizing not only the technology involved, but also the processes and procedures to develop, build and field those tools. Defense technology is known for being resistant to the application of new tools and procedures, as legacy systems and processes create inertia that makes it challenging to develop new technology in a timely manner.
Overcoming this challenge requires re-engineering workflows around current technology while enabling them to be adaptable to future technology. Industry and government both share a responsibility to make that happen; government must revamp its reliance on rigid, multi-year feature specifications, while industry must be ready to respond to changing demand signals and develop prototypes that are ready for edge applications on classified defense networks instead of simply developing prototypes in a sandbox.
“We need an ecosystem approach – taking commercial frontier models, wrapping them in defense-grade security and domain-specific knowledge, and embedding engineers alongside operators to continuously evolve the solutions,” said Berntsen. “When engineers and operators share the same feedback loop, we can move much faster as a living, strategic capability.”
What the future holds
Looking forward is never an exact science, as the technology of 10 years will certainly produce entirely unexpected advancements. Current and future conflicts have the potential to radically change what is needed, especially as domains such as space take on a more central role in warfighting.
But there are some well-informed speculations that can be made, Berntsen acknowledges. The first is a clearer delineation between purely automated and human-in-the-lead operations. While operational support tasks such as logistics, paperwork and intelligence sorting may be entirely automated – and are already heavily automated – critical decisions will stay with humans. The key differentiator between now and the future is a better understanding of what tasks can be safely automated or almost entirely automated, as agentic is still a new enough technology that identifying those tasks is an ongoing process.
Procurement will also change. Currently, the system is a multi-year cycle, where requirements are written, funding is requested, systems are built and then maintained indefinitely. Software development is an expensive endeavor, and SI-driven coding can cut that cost dramatically, enabling more bespoke software options instead of bigger-picture systems that are good at many tasks while not necessarily excelling at specific tasks.
“We won’t need to treat software as a permanent asset,” said Bernsten. “You build a capability for a specific mission problem, and if it stops being useful, you just turn it off and tear it down.”
The final shift that Berntsen envisions is pushing software skills directly to the front line, enabling front-line forces to respond quickly to new needs in the field. Instead of needing to request software support from headquarters or designated software developers, troops with software skills will be able to build apps or programs on the fly to meet their specific challenges.
“They build the digital capability on the spot, execute the mission, and tear it down,” said Berntsen. “That distributed, agile capability is what a modern force truly looks like.”

articles.title: Pentagon can’t track thousands of F-35 parts: GAO
articles.snippet: The government watchdog found that more than 17,000 F-35 fighter jet parts worth an estimated $1.3 billion were missing from the program’s inventory system.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The F-35 Joint Program Office cannot reliably track thousands of spare parts undergoing maintenance or repair, leaving officials without a clear picture on the location of as much as $2.5 billion worth of components across the aircraft’s global supply chain, according to a new government watchdog report.
The Government Accountability Office’s findings come against the backdrop of a Pentagon investigation into how F-35 components shipped from Australia to the United States ended up in Hong Kong, potentially exposing the jet’s secrets to the Chinese government. While GAO did not link the incident to inventory problems detailed in the report, the watchdog’s findings underscore the Pentagon’s broader challenges in tracking F-35 parts.
As of March 2026, when the GAO conducted its research, more than 17,000 F-35 Lightning II parts, worth an estimated $1.3 billion, were missing from the program’s inventory system. The value could be as high as $2.5 billion when accounting for missing cost information and other acquisition expenses, officials told GAO.
The gaps stem in part from incomplete contractor records that are not routinely integrated into the program’s inventory system, making it difficult for the JPO to determine what parts are available and where they are.
“Without accurate data in its [accountable property system of record] and properly executed inventory procedures for F-35 parts, DOD management will not have the information it needs to support warfighter readiness and reliable financial reporting,” the GAO said.
The F-35 comes in three primary variants that are operated by the Air Force, Marine Corps and Navy, as well as specialized configurations for 19 international customers. Lockheed Martin serves as the stealth fighter’s prime contractor, while RTX subsidiary Pratt & Whitney supplies its engine.
Overall, the F-35 program relies on over 1,900 domestic and 2,100 global suppliers, with approximately 26 million parts distributed across more than 700 contractor- and government-management facilities worldwide, per the GAO. The Defense Department uses the Enterprise Logistics Management System (ELMS) to manage the fighter jet’s sprawling inventory.
While the ELMS is able to capture real-time inventory changes, the platform cannot interface with property management systems run by Lockheed Martin and Pratt & Whitney — an issue first reported by GAO in 2022, which has persisted as of August 2026, according to the watchdog.
Instead, the JPO relies on periodic contractor data submissions and information from other Pentagon systems to update its records. Those submissions occur quarterly for the joint spare parts pool, meaning some inventory records can be more than three months old, GAO found.
Furthermore, the JPO lacks procedures to validate the accuracy of contractor data before entering it into the ELMS. A December 2025 submission included serial numbers for only 29 percent of parts records and National Stock Numbers for 43 percent. Some of those records indicated the components cost just one cent or less, which GAO said indicated possible data errors.
The program office has also struggled to verify how many F-35 parts are at facilities. Since fiscal 2020, the JPO has spent at least $17 million conducting inventories, but GAO found that its most recent effort did not fully verify that parts were physically in place or that inventory records accounted for all of them.
A JPO spokesperson told Breaking Defense that it was “actively working” to address the issues raised in the GAO report, including development of new procedures and training for officials responsible for government-owned property, while working to better monitor and analyze parts losses.
“The JPO is modernizing its property management infrastructure by establishing direct, real-time data interfaces between government and prime contractor systems. This integration directly addresses previous system gaps to ensure seamless accountability of F-35 spare parts,” the spokesperson said in a statement.
Lockheed Martin did not immediately return Breaking Defense’s requests for comment.
An Ongoing Concern
The report echoes concerns the watchdog has raised in previous reviews of the Pentagon’s costliest program. In 2023, GAO found that a prime contractor had lost more than 1 million F-35 parts worth over $85 million between May 2018 and October 2022.
By March 2026, the contractor had submitted about $28 million in loss reports covering the missing parts between 2012 and 2025. The Defense Contract Management Agency determined the contractor should be financially liable for about $6 million, but the JPO could not determine whether those reports included any of the losses identified in GAO’s earlier review because it had not kept records of outstanding cases, according to the latest report.
The accounting problems could also affect the Pentagon’s ability to keep the F-35 ready for operations, GAO warned. Without accurate inventory records, the department may struggle to determine which parts it needs and in what quantities.
That could complicate the Pentagon’s $13.7 billion Global Support Solution Reset strategy, which calls for additional investment to improve F-35 performance — including increasing spare parts availability. The watchdog cautioned that the Pentagon may be unable to identify its needs or account for additional parts purchased under the strategy.
In the report, GAO recommended that DoD strengthen its oversight of reported parts losses and establish clearer procedures, training and responsibilities for officials who track government-owned property. The Pentagon agreed with all four recommendations and said it was taking corrective actions.
The Defense Contract Audit Agency is also working with the JPO on a full inventory of F-35 parts, targeted for completion in March 2027.
Updated Nov. 9, 2026 at 3:34 PM with comment from the F-35 Joint Program Office.

articles.title: Korean Air Aerospace pushes forward with Collaborative Combat Aircraft plans
articles.snippet: “We delivered our CCA platform last year and will having flight tests at the end of this year,” Director of International Business for KE-ASD Haneul Kim confirmed.
articles.full_text:
DAEJEON, South Korea — Korean Air Aerospace Division (KE-ASD) is readying its Low Observable Wingman Uncrewed Aerial Vehicle System (LOWUS) loyal wingman drone to make its first flight by the end of this year, the company has announced.
During a visit to KE-ASD’s research and development facility in South Korea at the end of October, executives briefed media on the research and development activities conducted by the specialized aerospace and defense manufacturing business unit of Korean Air airline. That included discussing LOWUS, which the company plans to enter as its contender for South Korea’s upcoming Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) competition.
Like other media outlets, Breaking Defense accepted travel and accommodations from KE-ASD to attend the briefing.
“We delivered our CCA platform last year and will having flight tests at the end of this year,” Director of International Business for KE-ASD Haneul Kim confirmed, adding that that two technology demonstrator aircraft have been handed over to South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development (ADD).
Following the initial trials, LOWUS, which has a length of 10.4 meters (34.1 feet) and a wingspan of 9.4 meters, will enter a full-scale development program that is due to begin in 2029 to meet the anticipated South Korean government’s timeline for the CCA competition. The Korean government has not indicated when the competition will start, but the eventual CCA winner is expected to be deployed alongside manned platforms and later production blocks of the KF-21 fighter.
A 5,500-lbf turbofan engine being developed by the ADD and Hanwha is expected to be ready in 2032 for use with the LOWUS, enabling the CCA to fly at speeds of up to Mach 0.8 and stay aloft for up to three hours. This will replace the Ukrainian AI-222 engine that is powering the initial aircraft.
Jung told reporters that LOWUS will be equipped with an Active Electronically Scanned Array Radar and Electro Optical systems, with its initial mission set being reconnaissance and eventually expanded to include penetrating contested airspace ahead of manned aircraft for strike and other combat missions.
AI Pilot Program
On the software front, ADD has launched a project to develop an AI Pilot that will have AI-enabled air combat technologies, and Jung added that there are plans to retrofit and integrate the system into the LOWUS aircraft currently under development for flight demonstration.
KE-ASD has also invested significant effort into the development of AI-enabled drone swarm software, with the company successfully demonstrating its efforts in September at the 2026 Defense Drone Tech Fair in South Korea.
“A fleet of 22 drones autonomously carried out coordinated reconnaissance, high-maneuver swarm flight and precision strike missions, managed through Korean Air’s proprietary integrated battle management system,” said a KE-ASD social media post about the September demonstration.
Video from the event showed 22 drones moving into two separate swarms, with one acting as decoys to occupy a simulated adversary air defense system while the other swarm conducted an attack against a preset target by crashing into it in rapid succession.
“The system does more than provide voice updates based on a pre-set scenario: it uses AI to assess mission status in real time and communicate relevant updates. It can also retrieve drone status and weather information in response to user queries, making it optimized for operations in the field,” the post added.
KE-ASD’s Senior Manager for Systems Integration Sumno Jung said the technology demonstrators will be used for the flight tests which will then lead to Manned-Unmanned Teaming (MUM-T) trials with an ADD-operated KT-1 turboprop trainer that is scheduled to begin at the end of 2027.

articles.title: Army fields launched effects to 11 of 12 divisions, with Griffon Aerospace delivering the majority
articles.snippet: In line with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s 2025 Drone Dominance memo, the Army was directed to provide each headquarters division and multi-domain task force with launched effects.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Army has fielded launched effects to all but one of its headquarters divisions, with Griffon Aerospace supplying the majority of the systems, according to senior Army officials.
The unmanned systems have been delivered to 11 of its 12 HQ divisions and each multi-domain task force (MDTF), according to Lt. Col. Hunter Gray, product manager for launched effects under Program Acquisition Executive Maneuver Air. He told reporters Thursday that the effort is part of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s 2025 Drone Dominance memo, which directed the Army to provide each HQ division and MDTF with launched effects by the end of 2026.
The service plans to start providing the 12th and final division with launched effects next month, Gray said. He did not disclose what divisions have been fielded thus far, and the Army did not respond to queries on the matter by press time.
Launched effects are unmanned aircraft or payloads deployed from crewed aircraft, ground vehicles or maritime platforms to deliver various kinetic and non-kinetic capabilities. Depending on their range and payload, the systems can extend the reach of units and provide effects without putting personnel directly in harm’s way.
To meet its fielding goals, the Army turned to established industry partners with the capacity to deliver “mission-ready platforms” at scale, while leveraging commercial supply chains to keep up with demand, Gray said.
“That fit very well in alignment with the ongoing acquisition reform and the directives that we’ve seen in the robotic and autonomous systems space,” he said.
Ski Horrocks, the deputy program manager of unmanned aerial systems under PAE Maneuver Air, said Thursday that, in addition to the Army’s recent acquisition reform, industry has been able to provide launched effects at scale thanks to the DoD’s drone marketplace.
“The real magic behind the marketplace is all the rapid acquisition authorities and the contract vehicles,” he said. Because Other Transaction Authorities (OTAs) allow contracts to be awarded much more quickly than traditional FAR-based contracts, he explained that they have helped the Army “move fast” in scaling launched effects and other drone platforms to soldiers. OTAs are the go-to contract vehicle the Army uses to award vendors a spot on the marketplace.
Gray said that some vendors have been able to scale faster than others, with dual-use company Griffon Aerospace standing out because of both the demand for its systems and its ability to incorporate soldier feedback and deliver updated platforms shortly thereafter.
“That is the vendor that we’ve been able to scale the most based off of priority,” Gray said. Griffon is currently able to provide hundreds of systems per month to the Army, he added.
“From the time that we identified the need to scale to the time that the first tranche of systems was delivered was about three weeks,” Gray said, referring to Griffon’s systems. “Since then, we’ve continued to maintain a frequency of that feedback loop with that tech insertion cycle and [have] ordered more aircraft per cycle so that we can continue to responsibly scale the industrial base to demand.”
Gray did not disclose the total number of launched effects systems that have been delivered, but said the “majority” have been long-range capabilities provided by Griffon. Neither he nor Griffon President Jordan French would disclose all of the company’s platforms that have been fielded, but both said the Army has received systems from Griffon’s broader family of launched effects, including its Outlaw drone.
“To narrow in on a singular platform is not really how we look at acquiring systems,” Gray said.
The Army is also procuring a range of payload capabilities for its launched effects, rather than prioritizing one particular mission area. Gray said those include intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, electronic warfare and kinetic effects.
“The great thing about the way that these systems are designed and the way that they operate is that we can adjust the payloads based off of the user requirement in near real time,” he said. “The demand ebbs and flows based off of the concept of the operation of the unit that we’re dealing with.”
The comments come after the Army’s lead for Drone Dominance, Col. Gregory Merkl, told reporters in September that the service has enough systems to outfit each squad with small, one-way attack drones. However, the systems have not yet reached every squad, and the service lacks enough trained personnel to operate them, Merkl added.
As part of Hegseth’s Drone Dominance initiative, he mandated that every Army squad be equipped with small, one-way attack drones by the end of fiscal 2026. Merkl’s September comments suggest the service had not yet met that goal, despite having sufficient systems in its inventory.

articles.title: Defense industry takes aim at ‘right to repair’ as NDAA decision looms
articles.snippet: Proponents of “right to repair” say it will allow troops the ability to fix equipment in the field without needing to reach back out to a contractor, but industry is raising concerns about intellectual property.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — When Congress returns this week, leaders of the armed services committees will face a looming decision on “right to repair” legislation aimed at giving troops the ability to fix their equipment while deployed, but industry groups say the measure could have grave implications for intellectual property.
Both the House and Senate versions of the fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act contain similar provisions that would give the Defense Department “default government purpose rights” for technical data and software — a paradigm under which the department has access to technical data, can use it to repair equipment, and can share it with third parties doing work on government contracts.
Industry organizations contend those new regulations would let the government pass on trade secrets and other proprietary information to competitors, eroding a company’s technical edge.
Virginia Burger, a senior defense policy analyst for the Project on Government Oversight, said industry’s real primary interest is in preserving its bottom line.
Restrictions on technical data can leave the Pentagon reliant on the original manufacturer for repairs, maintenance and replacement parts because the department lacks the rights to share proprietary information with competing contractors. As a result, a 2025 Government Accountability Office report found that data-rights shortfalls can contribute to vendor lock, drive up program costs and lengthen repair timelines.
Default government purpose rights would open up competition and force incumbents to offer better pricing — particularly on lucrative sustainment contracts that make up 70 percent of major defense programs’ life-cycle costs, Burger told Breaking Defense in an interview.
“Something like ‘right to repair’ would be a major shift in that dynamic and give the military the upper hand when it comes to negotiating for repair costs,” Burger said. “It enables the Department of Defense to negotiate from a stronger position. And it decreases some of those monopolies that exist within contracts in the sustainment world.”
Technical data can include engineering drawings, manufacturing specifications and equipment manuals, while software rights can cover source code and related documentation. Under government purpose rights, the Pentagon would be able to share that information with other contractors for government work — excluding for commercial purposes, Matt Murphy, senior director of acquisition policy for the Aerospace Industries Association, said during an October event.
“If we go to default government purpose rights, what that could do for industry is disincentivize private funding of technology development because you’re surrendering IP to the government as a default,” he said. “When you look under the hood, it really is a pretty expansive authority for the government to share this information.”
The State Of Play
Both versions of the NDAA would provide the Pentagon with government purpose rights as the default, with companies only able to claim an exemption only if they prove “through clear and convincing evidence, entitlement to more restrictive rights.”
However, there are a few key differences between the House bill’s Section 861 and the Senate Armed Services Committee (SASC)-approved Section 804:
- The House language does not explicitly exclude commercial items and would apply only to future contracts.
- The Senate bill includes clawback provisions that would allow the government to reclaim funding from a company, should it find that the firm “unjustly” obtained more restrictive rights that resulted in it receiving a sole-source contract.
The right to repair provisions in the House and Senate versions of the FY27 NDAA received broad bipartisan support in the armed services committees, bringing together unlikely political allies.
Reps. Maggie Goodlander, D-N.H., and Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., sponsored the amendment that was added to the House NDAA via voice vote. Meanwhile, members of the Senate Armed Services Committee voted 27-0 to add right to repair language — which originated in a bill authored by Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Tim Sheehy, R-Mont. — to its version of NDAA.
“The military should be able to repair its own equipment without waiting weeks or months for defense contractors to do the job,” Warren said in a statement to Breaking Defense. “These bipartisan reforms would strengthen military readiness and save taxpayers billions. I’ll keep fighting to make sure these commonsense reforms become law.”
Typically, language included in both the House and Senate version of the NDAA is considered a slam dunk for inclusion into the final bill. But despite bipartisan backing, right to repair is expected to be one of the most fought-over portions of the FY27 NDAA, with trade organizations and oversight groups locked into a lobbying blitz as lawmakers and staff hammer out a compromise version of the legislation.
Sources told Breaking Defense that the final decision on whether to include the right to repair provisions — or some version of them — will likely rest with the chairmen and ranking members of the armed services committees, known as the Big Four.
In a Sept. 1 letter to the armed services committee chairmen and ranking members, a collection of 15 industry organizations — including AIA, the National Defense Industrial Association and US Chamber of Commerce — advocated for Congress to revert to more moderate language in Section 842 of the House Armed Services Committee’s chairman’s mark.
Those provisions would require the Pentagon to name an “Intellectual Property Ombudsman” who would provide “independent, non-binding guidance” to contracting officers and companies on intellectual property matters, according to the bill text. The legislation would also establish a mediation process through which the Defense Department and industry could resolve IP disputes without going to court.
The language in Section 842 “bring[s] government and industry to the table to settle IP disputes quickly in good faith,” the industry organizations stated in the letter. “Requiring default GPR for all contracts will hamper innovation and the Pentagon’s access to cutting-edge technologies by deterring companies from contracting with the Department.”
Most recently, the Professional Services Council — a trade group representing government contractors — sent a Nov. 4 letter to HASC and SASC leaders expressing support for Section 842 and opposition to House Section 861 and the Senate Section 804.
“These provisions raise concerns because they lack protections for privately developed technology, increase administrative and evidentiary burdens placed on contractors, and pose potential negative consequences for companies that develop and deliver innovative technologies to the defense market,” PSC CEO Jim Carroll wrote.
Meanwhile, POGO is arguing for the most aggressive outcome: A hybrid of both bills that includes the broad applicability of the House and the clawback mechanism written into the Senate version, it stated in a list of its NDAA policy recommendations published in September.
“I think that would be the best option,” Burger said. “I also think that’s probably the least likely because industry lobbies heavily against this, and defense contractors have an immense amount of influence and pull over these things.”
Given the bipartisan support, right to repair proponents are cautiously optimistic that some form of the House and Senate language will survive the conference process. But since right to repair provisions were stripped from the FY26 NDAA during the conference process, Burger said, “I don’t know if we can really assume that that’s a given.”
“That being said, my guess is they probably will pass something. Whether or not it is as strong … that those of us advocating for ‘right to repair’ want it to be, I think is the real question.”
Meanwhile, industry is hoping that there is still time to move the needle.
“What we’re trying to understand: Is it that this language is immovable to members of Congress? Or can we propose new paths forward that address our concerns with [government purpose rights]?” Parker Chapman, AIA’s senior director of legislative affairs, told Breaking Defense.
‘We’re Not Trying To Harm Industry’
Since the beginning of the Trump administration, Pentagon leaders have championed the right to repair as a vital tool for ensuring that troops have the technical data necessary to maintain and repair forward-deployed equipment. While in office, former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll led the charge as the department’s most vocal proponent before resigning in August.
“This is one of the most important things, and I don’t say this to be over the top,” Driscoll said in response to questions from Warren during a SASC hearing in May. “We, the US Army and the broader military must maintain the right to take advantage of all the new tools because if we don’t, our adversaries will, and we will be put at a meaningfully worse position.”
Following Driscoll’s departure from the Pentagon in August, senior leaders have said little about the specific right to repair policies in the draft NDAA bills.
The White House’s statement of policy on the House NDAA language commends Congress for advancing the right to repair issue, but stops short of specifically endorsing the Goodlander provisions, stating instead that the Pentagon looks forward to working with Congress to refine the language.
“The Administration is committed to partnering with Congress to guarantee that any right to repair requirements included in the FY 2027 NDAA balance the Department’s need for data delivery with preserving the intellectual capital of our industry partners,” the White House said in its July statement.
During an Oct. 20 event at the Hudson Institute, the Army’s chief legislative liaison, Jimmy Byrn, said that the service wants to guarantee that it gets the legislative authority to repair its equipment while ensuring that industry remains unscathed.
“I’m confident that we can get to a good place on this particular issue,” he said. “We’ve been listening to industry about it, doing industry working groups and that type of thing to make sure that we’re addressing issues there. The main thing I just want to put out is that we’re not trying to harm industry.”
Some in industry see the lack of explicit support for House Section 861 and the Senate Section 804 as a positive sign.
“In the conversations that we’ve had with the Department — it’s not like they’re saying we don’t like this at all — but they are recognizing that default government purpose rights is a very broad stroke approach to this problem, and isn’t exactly the solution that they’re looking for,” AIA’s Murphy told Breaking Defense in an interview.
RTX CEO Chris Calio said in an October earnings call that he believed the government and industry would ultimately find a solution on right to repair, but added that there needs to be a balance between industry’s need to safeguard IP and the needs of the customer.
“We want to be supportive of our customers and their sustainment needs, but we’re also going to need the kinds of protections around IP and protections around the investments that we’ve made,” he said.
For others in industry, the issue has a personal connection. Scott Sanders, Forterra’s chief growth officer, told Breaking Defense that his unit wasn’t allowed to make a simple part swap on a broken generator when he was an active duty Marine deployed to a forward operating base in the early 2010s.
“Fun fact: We did it anyway, and then got screamed at by someone,” he said.
But while he’s supportive of troops being able to repair equipment in the field, Sanders said industry needs more clarity on how certain parts of the NDAA language would be implemented. For instance, what constitutes a “clear and convincing argument” to allow contractors to retain data rights?
“I don’t think there’s an easy definition here, because right to repair for deployed generators or trucks is going to be different than small drones,” he said. “You’re going to have to do it on an individual basis on every contract, and you’re going to assume that like the contracting officer or the program manager … is going to have the technical skills to look at a big complex weapon system, and then define which of those parts should be right to repair and which should not.”
Mandating that defense companies provide more technical data isn’t a panacea for the Pentagon’s readiness issues, said Moshe Schwartz, a defense fellow for the Coalition for Common Sense in Government Procurement.
“The reason that we have poor readiness rates is not tech data rights. It is not intellectual property,” Schwartz said. “Even if the department had all of the tech data rights in the world, it would not meaningfully impact the readiness rates of our system.”
Instead, Schwartz argued that the Pentagon could be better served by updating its IT infrastructure, which has contributed to readiness snags such as a case two years ago where monthly parts orders from the Army were logged as being needed only every few months, delaying delivery of needed parts.
The department also needs to do a better job ensuring that it forms concrete contractual agreements with companies for the intellectual property that it does need, he said.
“There are things that they can do, short of seizing [all] data [by default],” he said. “What data do you need, and why do you need it? Frequently, I’ve heard people in the Department say, ‘Well, we need all the data for every contingency.’ Well, that’s not helpful.”
Carley Welch contributed to this story.

articles.title: DoD taps Viasat to field operations ‘center’ for Golden Dome satellite data relay network
articles.snippet: The ID/IQ contract to “design, field and scale” the Mission Operation Center for the Space Data Network Backbone is worth a maximum of $450 million.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON ― The Space Force, in “partnership” with the Pentagon’s Golden Dome office, has tapped Viasat to build a Missions Operation Center (MOC) to integrate multiple satellite constellations and manage data traffic through the nascent Space Data Network (SDN) Backbone, the service announced.
The company has been awarded an indefinite delivery/indefinite quantity contract with a ceiling of $450 million to “design, field, and scale” the center, Space Systems Command said in a Thursday press release. “In this role, Viasat, Inc. will serve as the network and mission system integration partner as SSC expands its open-architecture ecosystem across multiple space-segment providers.”
The MOC will serve as the central network orchestration hub for the SDN Backbone, a constellation of low Earth orbit satellites being built by SpaceX to provide high-speed, low-latency communications. The backbone constellation is designed as the glue connecting the Space Data Network’s broader architecture of disparate military, and eventually commercial, space-based sensor and communications satellites with decision-makers and weapons platforms. The network’s near-term focus will be on supporting the Trump administration’s Golden Dome missile defense initiative.
Network orchestration enables autonomous shifting of data among the various satellite constellations in various orbits and down to the multiple ground stations supporting them, allowing data to “hop” from one constellation to another in the event of a slowdown in transmission due to bandwidth congestion or adversary jamming.
In essence, the MOC will function as a modern-day, software-run equivalent to an old-time telephone exchange where multiple human operators patched together phone calls via cables and provided troubleshooting services when calls failed.
“The MOC will bring together mission integration, network operations, and data transport management across a growing multi-vendor architecture,” the SSC release said.
According to the release, the MOC will provid the SDN Backbone with:
- Multi-Vendor Orchestration: Integrates disparate satellite systems into a unified communications network.
- Multi-Domain Joint Connectivity: Supports high-speed, low-latency, and cyber-resilient data paths for users across air, land, sea, and space.
- Real-Time Priority Routing: Enables dynamic data management and routing based on mission priorities through network operations infrastructure.
“The MOC establishes the mission operations layer needed to integrate the diverse space data transport and space exchange systems being developed across related efforts,” said Lt. Col. Alexa Eggert, materiel leader for the SDN Backbone program at SSC’s Space Based Sensing and Targeting Portfolio Acquisition Executive office, in a statement. “By bringing the systems together in one place, it positions us to deliver a more integrated mission capability across multiple constellations and systems.”

articles.title: Data breach at hearing aid giant Amplifon impacts thousands
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The U.S arm of international hearing aid company Amplifon has been notifying customers about a data breach early this year that included medical information.
articles.full_text:
Data breach at hearing aid giant Amplifon impacts thousands
International healthcare company Amplifon said thousands of its U.S. customers had their Social Security numbers and medical information stolen during a cyberattack in February.
The Milan, Italy, company pairs patients in need of hearing aids and auditory assistance with device providers and services.
Amplifon began notifying state regulators of a data breach last week, telling Texas officials that 85,804 people were impacted by the security incident in addition to 1,027 people in Vermont. The company also filed breach notices in California.
In a breach notice on its U.S. website, Amplifon said it initially discovered suspicious activity on February 11, with an investigation later revealing the hackers had access to company files between January 18 and February 8.
The stolen data includes names, driver’s licenses, state IDs, medical information, health insurance data and financial information.
No hacking group has taken credit for the incident as of Monday.
Several class action law firms said the total number of victims is 1,332,826, but Amplifon did not respond to requests for confirmation.
Amplifon was founded in 1950 for World War II veterans suffering from hearing loss and expanded to the U.S., Asia and Africa — now covering more than 28 countries across five continents. The company works with patients to find the right hearing devices and offer tests as well as other hearing-related healthcare services.
The healthcare industry, particularly companies producing wearable devices, has faced an unprecedented level of attack in 2026 by cybercriminals. Medical device maker iRhythm said last month that 8,179,772 people were impacted by a cyberattack on their systems.
Medical device makers like Medtronic, Boston Scientific, Stryker, UFP, Masimo, Surmodics, Artivion and Zoll have dealt with cybersecurity incidents that exposed the sensitive medical data of millions and caused supply chain issues.
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: Vanderbilt cybersecurity incident impacting campus devices and systems
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Vanderbilt University announced a cyberattack, warning students and employees that campus devices and systems may be impacted by the incident.
articles.full_text:
Vanderbilt cybersecurity incident impacting campus devices and systems
Vanderbilt University announced a cyberattack on Monday morning, warning students and employees that campus devices and systems may be impacted by the incident.
A spokesperson for the Nashville-based university told Recorded Future News their IT team is “actively investigating and working to contain the situation.”
Vanderbilt University posted a longer statement on social media asking everyone to shut down their devices, disconnect from university WiFi, and “remain extremely vigilant.”
They warned that anyone who notices suspicious activity on their devices — like pop-ups, security warnings, changes to files and password requests — should turn the device off and report it to campus IT officials.
Vanderbilt University, one of the premiere higher education institutions in the country, serves about 14,000 students and has more than 6,000 staff members.
Vanderbilt University Medical Center was previously attacked by a ransomware gang in 2023.
The attack emerged early Monday after the ransomware gang BYOD added the university to its leak site and made several claims about stolen data.
The group has staged several high-profile attacks in recent weeks, including an incident involving Michigan State University and the University of New Mexico.
The attack on the University of New Mexico caused alarm because it also impacted the school’s medical facilities, forcing one of the state’s only top-tier hospitals to turn away ambulances.
Ransomware expert Allan Liska said BYOD has been ramping up as of late but only emerged recently.
“We didn’t see their first victim until Sept 29th,” he said.
The group is believed to have carried out an attack on Trump Mobile and to have subsequently leaked data from 3,615 prominent customers, which drew Congressional scrutiny.
Multiple cybersecurity firms released reports last week warning of startling increases in ransomware attacks this year as artificial intelligence tools proliferate across the cybercriminal ecosystem.
Halcyon said it saw a 40% increase in ransomware activity between July and September – with 111 groups claiming 2,766 attacks against organizations in 122 countries.

Ukraine arrests four in $5 million crypto scam targeting Germans
Ukrainian police have arrested four people suspected of running a network of fraudulent call centers that stole millions of euros from German citizens by luring them into fake cryptocurrency investments.
The arrests come as Kyiv steps up efforts to crack down on illegal call centers, some of which have allegedly operated under the protection of corrupt law enforcement officials.
In a statement Friday, Ukraine's cyber police said the suspects operated call centers across the country, posing as financial advisers and persuading people in the European Union, particularly Germany, to invest in cryptocurrencies and stocks through fraudulent online platforms.
After gaining victims' trust, the scammers helped them open cryptocurrency exchange accounts and transfer funds to wallets controlled by the criminal group. In some cases, they also gained access to victims' online banking accounts.
The stolen funds were then moved through a network of bank accounts and cryptocurrency wallets to conceal their origins before being distributed among members of the group, police said.
Investigators have identified 135 victims in Germany who collectively lost more than €4.3 million ($4.8 million).
Ukrainian authorities conducted two rounds of raids in August and September, searching more than 50 properties in Kyiv and other cities. Officers seized computers, phones, cryptocurrency wallets, documents and more than $90,000 in cash.
The four arrests included the group’s alleged leader. Three men are being held in pretrial detention, while a suspected co-organizer has been placed under house arrest.
Video released by police showed one suspect hiding on an apartment balcony during a raid, while another attempted to escape.
The suspects face up to 12 years in prison and confiscation of their property if convicted. Investigators are still working to identify other members of the network and additional victims.
Broader crackdown
The arrests come amid a broader push by Ukrainian authorities to combat fraudulent call centers.
In September, Ukraine's parliament approved legislation introducing specific criminal penalties for organizing or operating scam call centers, working at them or recruiting people to participate in fraudulent schemes. The legislation provides for prison sentences of up to 12 years for certain offenses linked to such operations.
The crackdown has also exposed alleged corruption within Ukraine's own security and law enforcement agencies.
Last week, Ukrainian anti-corruption investigators said they had uncovered a criminal organization that allegedly bribed senior officials to protect fraudulent call centers from investigations.
The alleged network involved at least 12 people, including officials from Ukraine's Security Service (SBU), the Prosecutor General's Office and the National Police, as well as individuals linked to organized crime.
Following the investigation, the SBU dismissed two senior officials suspected of involvement in the scheme.

articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Hackers allegedly assisted by AI breached a German web hosting company through a tool designed to allow customers to connect AI assistants to their accounts, the company disclosed.

Alleged AI-aided cyberattack exploits assistant interface to breach German web host
Hackers allegedly assisted by AI breached a German web hosting company through a tool designed to allow customers to connect AI assistants to their accounts, the company disclosed over the weekend.
Mittwald CM Service, a hosting provider for web agencies based in North Rhine-Westphalia, disclosed in a blog post Saturday that hackers had compromised 56 customer projects after going undetected on its systems for eight days.
The company’s managing director Robert Meyer said the attackers exploited a flaw in Mittwald’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) server used to allow customers to connect their AI assistants to mStudio, a platform for managing websites and hosting services. It is unclear whether the flaw was in the company’s own code or in the open-source MCP software libraries.
Meyer said the attacker appeared to have used AI tools in the breach, explaining the company’s logs “show that he worked his way through our system extremely quickly” and that “in some cases, only seconds passed between steps that would take significantly longer for a human attacker.”
Mittwald provided no other evidence of AI involvement. The company did not immediately respond when asked to distinguish between the detection of AI tools and conventional scripts that also allow hackers to move faster than an unaided human operator.
According to Mittwald’s own timeline, the attacker first tested the MCP flaw amid a global scramble in October to apply patches for PHP2Shell. Meyer said “the attacker disguised his access attempts and carried out various diversionary tactics.”
“External IT forensic experts are continuously supporting us with the analysis. We have informed the relevant authorities,” Meyer said.
After forensic evaluations of the 56 compromised projects, and repeated scans of Mittwald's own systems, the company said that as of Friday it could not detect any additional attacker activity.
“First the PHP2Shell vulnerability, now the attack on our systems. AI attacks will become more frequent in the future,” Meyer wrote. “We want to be transparent about this, and therefore we will publish a detailed account of the events next week, as soon as our analysis and recovery are complete. We will be working on this throughout the weekend and beyond.”

articles.title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
articles.snippet: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder's web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
articles.full_text:
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.
The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.
Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.
Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.
“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.
“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”
All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.
As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

articles.title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
articles.snippet: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user's Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet's access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
articles.full_text:
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).
The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”
The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.
Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).
The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.
Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.
Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.
Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.
In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.
Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.
That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.
Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linus Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links].
The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”
Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”
“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”
Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.
“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”
The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.
“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”

articles.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
articles.snippet: Expect to see quite a few websites serving "404" or "Page Not Found" errors today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
articles.full_text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.
Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.
OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”
Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.
Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].
“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”
The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.
The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.
According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.
“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”
The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.
This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.
Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.
